the time interval between the anaesthesia and irradiations of mouse mammary tumour xenografts is a key factor in the radiation response.

the effect of the anaesthetic on the radiation response of tumours.
the study of the radiation response of tumours, with particular emphasis on the effects of anaesthesia and the influence of oxygen.

the anaesthetic agents used in these experiments, when used in the manner described, do not sensitize mouse tumours to the effects of radiation.

the radiation response of mouse tumours in oxygen can be significantly modified by anaesthesia, but only if the interval between administration of the anaesthetic and irradiation of the tumours is short (less than 10 min).
the use of anaesthesia for irradiating tumours in mice should be avoided, if possible, or at least the time between anaesthesia and the start of irradiation should be kept to a minimum.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the radiation response of mouse tumours is not affected by ketamine and/or diazepam anaesthesia if the time interval between the administration of anaesthetic and irradiation is less than 10 min.

the radiation sensitivity of C3H mammary tumours was reduced in anaesthetized mice compared with non-anaestheized mice, and the sensitivity was increased by irradiation in oxygen at 1 atm compared with air.

the radiation response of mouse tumours is influenced by anaesthesia and the time interval between administration of the anaesthetic and irradiation, the magnitude of the effect depending on the radiation dose, oxygen concentration and the anaesthetic used.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the time interval between the administration of anaesthetic and radiation should be kept to a minimum, especially when irradiating in pure oxygen.
anaesthesia of the host mouse is a factor that must be considered in the experimental design of radiation studies of mouse tumours.
anaesthesia should be given as late as possible before irradiation of mouse mammary tumour cells.
